what.label: supported
what.says: The canal joins the Gulf of Corinth to the Saronic Gulf; completed in 1893, it cuts through the Isthmus and separates the Peloponnese from the mainland.
quote: connects the Gulf of Corinth in the Ionian Sea with the Saronic Gulf in the Aegean Sea. Completed in 1893, it cuts through the narrow Isthmus of Corinth and separates the Peloponnese peninsula from the Greek mainland.

island.label: supported
island.says: Wikivoyage says the canal arguably makes the Peloponnese an island.
quote: separating the Peloponnese from the Greek mainland, arguably making the peninsula an island.

size.label: supported
size.says: It is 6.4 km long and 24.6 m wide at the surface; the walls rise 90 m (300 ft) above sea level at a near-vertical 80 degrees.
quote: It is 6.4 kilometres (4 miles) in length
24.6 metres (81 ft) in breadth at the surface
The rock walls, which rise 90 metres (300 ft) above sea level, are at a near-vertical 80° angle.

bridges.label: estimate
bridges.says: A railway, a road and a motorway cross at a height of about 45 m.
quote: The canal is crossed by a railway line, a road, and a motorway at a height of about 45 metres (148 ft).

no-locks.label: supported
no-locks.says: It was dug at sea level and has no locks.
quote: The canal was dug through the Isthmus at sea level and has no locks.

periander.label: supported
periander.says: The idea began with Periander of Corinth in the 7th century BC, who built the Diolkos instead.
quote: The Corinth canal concept originated with Periander of Corinth in the 7th century BC. Daunted by its enormity, he chose to implement the Diolkos, a land trackway for transporting ships, instead.

periander-why.label: disputed
periander-why.says: His change of mind is put down variously to cost, lack of labor, or fear of losing Corinth's role as a trading hub.
quote: Periander's change of heart is attributed variously to the great expense of the project, a lack of labour or a fear that a canal would have robbed Corinth of its dominant role as an entrepôt for goods.

curse.label: legend
curse.says: Apollonius of Tyana prophesied illness for anyone who proposed a canal; Plutarch and Suetonius wrote that Caesar considered one but was assassinated first.
quote: The philosopher Apollonius of Tyana prophesied that anyone who proposed to dig a Corinthian canal would be met with illness.
the historians Plutarch and Suetonius both wrote that the Roman dictator Julius Caesar considered digging a canal through the isthmus but was assassinated before he could begin the project.

nero.label: supported
nero.says: Nero broke ground himself with a pickaxe in 67 AD; the work stopped when he died; 6,000 Judean prisoners of war did the digging.
quote: The emperor Nero was the first to attempt to construct the canal, personally breaking the ground with a pickaxe and removing the first basket-load of soil in 67 AD, but the project was abandoned when he died shortly afterwards.
The Roman workforce, consisting of 6,000 Judean prisoners of war

nero-course.label: supported
nero-course.says: A relief of Hercules left by Nero's workers is on the north side of the cutting at the Gulf of Corinth end; the modern canal follows Nero's course.
quote: A memorial of the attempt in the form of a relief of Hercules was left by Nero's workers and can be seen in the north side of the canal cutting today, at the Gulf of Corinth end, below an old bridge foundation. The modern canal follows the same course as Nero's.

modern.label: supported
modern.says: Work restarted in 1881 but geological and financial problems bankrupted the builders; it was finished on 25 July 1893.
quote: Construction finally recommenced in 1881 but was hampered by geological and financial problems that bankrupted the original builders.
was completed on 25 July 1893

unstable.label: supported
unstable.says: The walls have been unstable from the start; in 1923 alone 41,000 cubic metres fell into the canal.
quote: The canal's high limestone walls have been persistently unstable from the start.
In 1923 alone, 41,000 cubic metres of material fell into the canal, which took two years to clear out.

closures.label: supported
closures.says: It closed at the start of 2021 after a landslide and reopened on 1 June 2023.
quote: The canal closed at the beginning of 2021 after a landslide.
the canal reopened on June 1, 2023.

ww2.label: supported
ww2.says: In October 1944 retreating German forces blocked the canal; it reopened to all traffic in 1948.
quote: In October 1944, as German forces retreated from Greece, the canal was put out of action by German "scorched earth" operations.
reopened it for shallow-draft traffic by 7 July 1948, and for all traffic by that September.

today.label: estimate
today.says: It saves a 700 km trip around the Peloponnese, is mostly used by tourist ships, around 15,000 a year, and is of little economic importance.
quote: The canal saves a 700-kilometre (430 mi) journey around the Peloponnese for transiting vessels.
The canal is currently used mainly by tourist ships; around 15,000 ships per year
It is currently of little economic importance and is mainly a tourist attraction.
it is impassable for many modern ships

sinking.label: supported
sinking.says: Since 1988 submersible bridges sit at sea level at each end, by Isthmia in the east and Poseidonia in the west.
quote: In 1988, submersible bridges were installed at sea level at each end of the canal, by the eastern harbour of Isthmia and the western harbour of Poseidonia

diolkos.label: supported
diolkos.says: The Diolkos was a paved trackway that let boats be moved overland across the Isthmus, from about 600 BC to the middle of the first century AD.
quote: was a paved trackway near Corinth in Ancient Greece which enabled boats to be moved overland across the Isthmus of Corinth
operated from c. 600 BC until the middle of the first century AD

fast.label: supported
fast.says: Aristophanes wrote 'as fast as a Corinthian', showing the trackway was famous for speed.
quote: The phrase "as fast as a Corinthian", penned by the comic playwright Aristophanes, indicates that the trackway was common knowledge and had acquired a reputation for swiftness.

grooves.label: supported
grooves.says: It was paved with hard limestone with parallel grooves about 1.60 m apart.
quote: The Diolkos was a trackway paved with hard limestone with parallel grooves running about 1.60 metres (63 in) apart.

hauling.label: estimate
hauling.says: Ships were presumably pulled by men and animals with ropes; one estimate for a warship is a team of 112 to 142 people.
quote: Ship and cargo were presumably pulled by men and animals with ropes, tackles and possibly also capstans.
must have numbered between 112 and 142 people
The tracks indicate that transport on the Diolkos was done with some sort of wheeled vehicle.

remains.label: supported
remains.says: Remains survive next to the canal, mainly at the western end; erosion from ships has left much of it in poor shape; a walkway surrounds it at the western end, east of the lowering bridge.
quote: Remnants of the Diolkos still exist next to the modern canal.
Today, erosion caused by ship movements on the nearby Canal has left considerable portions of the Diolkos in a poor state, particularly at its excavated western end.
This surround and walkway is on both sides of the road at the western end of the canal, east of the lowering-bridge.

parts.name: On the bridge
parts.stand: On the walkway of a bridge over the canal, partway across, looking down into the cutting.

paras.t: First, hold on to the railing and keep a firm grip on your phone and anything you're carrying. It's a long way down.

Below you is the Corinth Canal, finished in 1893. It slices through the Isthmus, joining the Gulf of Corinth on one side to the Saronic Gulf on the other. It cut the Peloponnese off from the mainland, so you could argue that southern Greece is now an island.

Look at those walls. They rise 90 metres, about 300 feet, above the sea, at a near-vertical angle of 80 degrees. The bridges cross at a height of about 45 metres. And yet the canal is only 24.6 metres wide at the surface, and 6.4 kilometres long. It was dug at sea level, so there are no locks at all.

parts.name: A very old dream
parts.stand: Stay at the railing and look along the canal toward the far end.

paras.t: People dreamed of this cut for some two and a half thousand years. The first was Periander, ruler of Corinth in the 7th century BC. He gave up, and built a stone ship road across the land instead, the Diolkos.
Why did he give up? Nobody knows for sure. It may have been the cost, or a lack of workers, or a fear that a canal would take trade away from Corinth itself.

The idea seemed cursed. The story goes that the philosopher Apollonius of Tyana warned that anyone who proposed a canal would fall ill. Plutarch and Suetonius both wrote that Julius Caesar considered one, but was assassinated before he could begin.

The emperor Nero actually started. In 67 AD he broke the ground himself with a pickaxe. The digging was done by 6,000 Judean prisoners of war. When Nero died soon after, the work stopped. But today's canal follows the same line as his.
His workers left a relief of Hercules carved into the rock. It's on the north side of the cutting, at the Gulf of Corinth end, below an old bridge foundation.

parts.name: Building it, and keeping it open
parts.stand: Look down at the walls, at the lines and scars in the rock.

paras.t: Work started again in 1881, and it was a struggle. Rock and money troubles bankrupted the original builders. The canal was finally completed on 25 July 1893.

Those walls have never been stable. In 1923 alone, 41,000 cubic metres of rock fell into the water. More recently, a landslide closed the canal at the start of 2021, and it only reopened on 1 June 2023.
War hit it too. In October 1944, retreating German forces put the canal out of action, and it didn't reopen to all traffic until 1948.

Today it's mostly a sight in itself. It saves ships a 700 kilometre trip around the Peloponnese, but it's too narrow for many modern ships. Around 15,000 ships a year still squeeze through, mostly tourist boats. At each end there's a bridge that sinks under the water to let them pass.

parts.name: The Diolkos
parts.stand: If you go on to the western end of the canal, by the sinking bridge, look for the old stone roadway beside the water.

paras.t: Before the canal, there was the Diolkos: a paved road for dragging boats across the Isthmus. It ran from about 600 BC to the middle of the first century AD. Pieces of it survive next to the canal, mostly at this western end.

Look for the grooves in the hard limestone, about 1.6 metres apart. Ships were presumably hauled on some sort of wheeled vehicle, pulled by men and animals with ropes. One estimate says a warship needed a team of some 112 to 142 people. It worked well enough that the playwright Aristophanes joked about something being "as fast as a Corinthian."
Please keep to the walkway. Ships passing in the canal have eroded much of the old road, and it's fragile.

Stand between the two for a moment: the ancient stone road and the modern cut beside it. Two and a half thousand years of people looking at the same narrow strip of land, and refusing to sail the long way round.
